question: Following a meeting on 15 February 2024, Spain’s Railway Accident Investigation Committee (CIAF) announced that it had ruled out a new investigation into the rail accident that took place in Santiago on 24 July 2013 and resulted in 81 deaths, in spite of the Commission’s requests.

According to CIAF, opening a new investigation into an event already investigated would be unfounded in the absence of new evidence or unaddressed factors from which to draw new lessons and recommendations for improving the safety of the railway system. This is a regrettable decision constituting a lack of respect for victims.

What is more, in 2016, the European Union Agency for Railways stated in its report on this accident that CIAF’s 2014 investigation was not independent and did not address the root causes of the accident or safety factors. The agency called for changes to be made. In 2017, the Commission’s Directorate-General for Mobility and Transport called on CIAF to carry out an independent investigation. 1.
Can the Commission confirm whether it has contacted the competent Spanish authorities about CIAF’s decision?
Will it call on CIAF, once again, to carry out an independent investigation, as Commissioner Violeta Bulc did previously?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.6.2024) Under the existing legislative framework, the Commission’s role is limited. In accordance with Article 20 of Directive 2016/7981 the obligation to ensure that an investigation is carried out after any serious accident on the Union rail system rests fully with the Member States.

Such investigation shall be conducted by the national independent body established by the Member State in accordance with Article 22 of that Directive. The Commission would also like to refer to its answer to a previous written question investigation by the national investigating body. The decision to reopen an investigation lies exclusively with the Spanish Railway Accident Investigation Committee (CIAF).
